title: The gold test
hook: Titan built a jewellery plant to sell to Europe, but Europe did not buy. Can you sell gold to India instead?
role: You lead Titan's jewellery business, 1994 to 2003

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: Money the jewellery business makes today

future.label: Trust
future.hint: How much Indian families trust Tanishq with their gold

intro.text: Hosur, 1994. Titan, the Tata company that makes India's best-selling watches, has built a ₹65 crore jewellery plant here to sell to Europe. The idea grew out of 1990–91, when India was short of the dollars it needed to buy from abroad, but the orders from Europe never came. Now you must make money from the plant in India, under a new name: Tanishq.

s_goal.text: In India, families save money by buying gold. More than two-thirds of the jewellery made here is for weddings, and families buy it from a jeweller they have trusted for years. They want 22-karat gold, which is almost pure. Your plant, however, was built for light 18-karat pieces that are only three-quarters gold.

d1.title: A plant built for Europe
d1.setup: You have a plant, a famous parent company and no shops. Your team dreams of a brand like the great jewellers of Europe, with diamonds, new designs and elegant stores. The plant is ready to make that jewellery today.
d1.question: How do you launch your jewellery in India?
d1.advisor: Every jeweller in India sells the same heavy gold. A brand that looks different will get noticed.

options.label: Launch 18-karat diamond jewellery in elegant stores. It stands out, but it's new to Indian buyers.
options.outcome: No test is done. In July 1996 Tanishq opens its first store on Cathedral Road in Chennai: a quiet, European-style shop full of 18-karat diamond jewellery, where buyers must book a visit before they come in. For most of that first year, almost nobody comes in.
options.why: Remember: ask what they did last time, never "would you buy?" Nobody asked families what gold they had bought for their last wedding. You built the launch around what your plant could make, not what buyers already bought.
options.better: Find out what families really bought last time: 22-karat gold, from a jeweller they trusted. Lead with that, and add your designs on top.
options.takeaway: In 1994 you launched a product without asking customers if they wanted it.

options.label: Spend months visiting jewellers to see what families really buy. You learn, but the plant waits.
options.outcome: For a few months your team visits families and jewellers and watches what people really buy. The answer is clear: 22-karat gold, for weddings and for savings. Craftsmen in other cities help your plant make it, and in 1996 you open later than planned, but your first store sells what people came looking for.
options.why: Remember: ask what they did last time, never "would you buy?" What families had bought, again and again, was 22-karat gold. A few slow months showed you the market you were entering, not the one you had planned for in Europe.
options.takeaway: In 1994 you watched what buyers really bought before you built the shop.

options.label: Show your designs to shoppers, and launch if most say they would buy. It's quick and cheap.
options.outcome: Most shoppers say the designs are lovely and they would buy them. So you launch mostly 18-karat jewellery, with a small 22-karat line because a few people asked for it. Your first store opens in Chennai in 1996.
options.why: Remember: ask what they did last time, never "would you buy?" Shoppers can say they like a design without spending any money. What families had actually bought, 22-karat gold from a jeweller they trusted, was what you needed to know.
options.better: Watch what families really bought last time, then put most of your stock into 22-karat gold.
options.takeaway: In 1994 you asked shoppers if they would buy, and they said yes to be kind.

d2.title: The empty store

setup.text: It is 1996. In your Chennai store the few 22-karat pieces sell, but the 18-karat diamond pieces don't. Your staff hear the same request every day: give us more 22-karat gold. Craftsmen in other cities could make it quickly. But your designers say the 18-karat diamond pieces are what make Tanishq different, and your plant was built to make them.

It is 1996. Your first store in Chennai is beautiful and almost empty. From the few people who do come in, your staff keep hearing the same thing: we need 22-karat jewellery. Craftsmen in other cities could make it quickly. But your designers say the 18-karat diamond pieces are what make Tanishq different, and your plant was built to make them.

d2.question: What do you put on your shelves?
d2.advisor: Our designers built something no one else in India has. If we copy the local jewellers, why would anyone pick us?

options.label: Make 22-karat gold your main range. More families may come, but your 18-karat stock sells at a loss.
options.outcome: You rebuild the range around 22-karat gold, your plant learns to make it, and the stores feel open to everyone. Much of your 18-karat stock is sold at a loss, and some designers are unhappy. But more families walk in, and they start to see you as a jeweller for people like them.
options.why: Remember: new must be far better than old, or fit old habits. Families had saved in 22-karat gold all their lives. Selling your old stock at a loss was costly, but now buyers could keep buying gold the way they always had.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you took a loss to sell what buyers already trusted.

options.label: Add more 22-karat pieces from outside craftsmen. Diamonds stay the star, but your shelves are split.
options.outcome: Your team gets 22-karat jewellery made by craftsmen in Mumbai and Mysore, and many more people walk in. But most of the range is still 18-karat diamonds, and the Chennai store ends its first year at ₹2.8 crore of sales, short of the ₹3.5 crore it aimed for.
options.why: Remember: new must be far better than old, or fit old habits. The 22-karat pieces let families buy the way they always had, so more people came in. But most of your shelves still asked them to change how they buy gold.
options.better: Make 22-karat gold the main range, not a side line, and make the stores feel open to everyone.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you fixed part of the problem and left the rest.

options.label: Keep only 18-karat and trust your designers. Your brand stays clear, but sales may stay slow.
options.outcome: You support your team, and your ads explain why 18-karat is the world standard. But families don't want to change the way they save in gold. Few people visit the store, and your losses grow.
options.why: Remember: new must be far better than old, or fit old habits. For a family that saves in gold, 18-karat was not far better than 22-karat, because it held less gold. Supporting your team meant asking every buyer to change an old habit, and that takes years.
options.better: Give buyers the 22-karat gold they keep asking for.
options.takeaway: In 1996 you stood by your product and asked buyers to change instead.

text.text: It is 1997. Your 22-karat gold sells, but buyers keep asking one question: how do I know it is really 22-karat? Every jeweller in India promises the same thing.
It is 1997. Your new 22-karat range brings families in, but they keep asking one question: how do I know your gold is really 22-karat? Every jeweller promises the same thing.
It is 1997. Your 18-karat stores are still quiet, and the losses keep growing. The board wants to hear what will make buyers choose you over the jeweller they already know.

It is 1997, and Tanishq lost ₹10.6 crore last year. Your own annual report now says that Indians strongly prefer 22-karat gold, and that many buyers get less gold than they paid for. You add more 22-karat jewellery, and your price tags now show the weight of the gold and the making charge, the fee for making the piece, as two separate amounts.
It is 1997. More 22-karat pieces help, but buyers still trust their old family jeweller more than a new brand, and your losses keep growing.

d3.title: The gold-testing machine
d3.setup: Many jewellers sell 19 or 20-karat gold but call it 22-karat. Everyone in the trade knows it, and many buyers suspect it, but a buyer can only check by melting the piece. At a show in Basel, Switzerland, your head of manufacturing saw a machine that reads the gold in a piece in about three minutes, without harming it. Each costs more than ₹10 lakh, and you are losing money.
d3.question: What do you do with the machine?
d3.advisor: If we prove our gold is pure, we also prove that other jewellers' gold is not. They won't forgive us for that.

options.label: Keep it in your factory so all your gold is perfect. Jewellers stay calm, but it costs ₹10 lakh.
options.outcome: Your own gold is always right, your staff can say so, and the other jewellers leave you alone. But buyers never see the proof, so your promise sounds like every other jeweller's, and the money spent on the machine shows them nothing.
options.why: Remember: let buyers check your promise for themselves. Your gold was honest, but only you could see it, and a promise buyers can't check sounds the same as everyone else's.
options.better: Put the machine in the store, where customers can watch their own gold being tested.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you kept your proof in the factory, where no buyer could see it.

options.label: Try one machine in one store first. It's a cheap test, but the other stores wait a year.
options.outcome: One machine goes into the Chennai store. People stand in line to test their gold, and many are shocked by what they learn. A year later you put machines in every store, but for that year, buyers everywhere else still had to trust your word.
options.why: Remember: let buyers check your promise for themselves. Trying something in one store first is usually wise, but the cheating was already well known. In every store without a machine, buyers still had to trust your word.
options.better: Put the machines in every store at once, so buyers everywhere can check your gold.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you tested in one store when buyers everywhere needed the proof.

options.label: Put machines in every store and test anyone's gold free. Buyers see proof, but jewellers get angry.

outcome.text: Crowds come to test their gold, and many are shocked to learn how little of it is pure. They leave knowing your gold is honest, but there is no 22-karat gold on your shelves for them to buy, so most of them walk out empty-handed.

From 1997 the machines go into Tanishq stores across India, and the ad company Lintas names them the Karatmeter. Anyone can test their gold free, even gold bought elsewhere. Hundreds stand in line, and some cry when they see how little gold their jewellery holds. Local jewellers pressure your shop owners, some even threatening to hurt them, and purity becomes the heart of your ads.

options.why: Remember: let buyers check your promise for themselves. You helped buyers see a problem they could not see before, and test your promise with their own eyes. Jewellers who sold less gold than they promised could not offer the same proof.
options.takeaway: In 1997 you let customers prove your promise themselves.

text.text: It is 2000, and you now have about 30 stores. Sales have grown more than four times in three years, but Tanishq has lost money every year. In May, Titan puts a new managing director above you. The next day your head of operations quits with six senior staff, and then the whole sales and marketing team leaves. You must hire a new team.

It is 2000, and you now have about 30 stores. Buyers never liked your 18-karat jewellery, so under pressure from the board you have finally added 22-karat gold, years late. Then Titan puts a new managing director above you, and many senior staff quit. The stores are still yours to run, but you must hire a new team.

It is 2000, and you now have about 30 stores. Your losses keep growing, and buyers still have no reason to leave their family jeweller. Then Titan puts a new managing director above you, and many senior staff quit. The stores are still yours to run, but you must hire a new team.

It is 2000, and you now have about 30 stores. Sales are growing, but the business is still losing money. Then Titan puts a new managing director above you, and many senior staff quit. The stores are still yours to run, but you must hire a new team.

d4.title: Too few buyers

setup.text: Too few people visit your stores. Your new team asks buyers why, and they give three reasons: many don't know Tanishq, some think it costs too much, and others feel the stores are only for rich people.

d4.question: How do you get people through the door?
d4.advisor: A shop can't sell to people who never come in. But if the brand starts to feel cheap, will wealthier buyers still want it?

options.label: Run a big TV campaign in your usual style. All of India learns your name, but it costs a lot.
options.outcome: The new ads make Tanishq famous, but they still look like ads for a luxury shop. Buyers who felt shut out still feel shut out, and your cash runs low.
options.why: Remember: a cheap first offer pays only if enough buyers return and pay full price. More ads gave no one an easy, low-cost reason to visit. The problem was what your ads said, not how many people saw them.
options.better: Give people one easy, low-cost reason to visit, like a birthday sale with low-priced pieces.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you made the brand famous without making it feel open to more people.

options.label: Hold a birthday sale from ₹399. Crowds may come, but rich buyers may think you're cheap.

outcome.text: Tanishq's birthday offer brings big crowds. Your ads now show real bracelets, rings and chains, and a range from ₹399 tells buyers that Tanishq is for them too. Collections for working women and sales to companies follow, and in 2000–01 Tanishq makes its first profit.
The birthday offer brings big crowds, and your ads now show real pieces. A range from ₹399 tells buyers that Tanishq is for them too, and for the first time your stores feel busy.

options.why: Remember: a cheap first offer pays only if enough buyers return and pay full price. A ₹399 piece was a cheap first step into the shop, and a jeweller can afford that because a family that trusts you comes back for every wedding, at full price.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you gave buyers a cheap first visit, so they could come back for more.

options.label: Close the weak stores and keep the big-city ones. Losses shrink, but fewer families meet you.
options.outcome: Your losses get smaller, but so does the brand, and families in smaller cities never get to know you.
options.why: Remember: a cheap first offer pays only if enough buyers return and pay full price. Shrinking cut your losses, but it gave nobody a first reason to come in. Fewer stores meant fewer families who would ever come back.
options.better: Keep the stores open, and give people a low-cost reason to visit.
options.takeaway: In 2000 you shrank to survive instead of fixing why buyers stayed away.

text.text: By 2002 your stores are busy, and Tanishq has made a small profit two years running. But in 2002 Indians buy about a fifth less gold than in 2001, so every new family counts.
By 2002 your stores are busy, and the business makes a small profit. But most families still keep their gold with the old family jeweller.
By 2002 everyone knows the name Tanishq, but the stores are still too quiet, and cash is running low.
By 2002 your losses are small, but you sell only in a few big cities. Most families have never walked into a Tanishq store.

d5.title: Turn the test into a sale

setup.text: By 2002 you have moved the machines into your stores, and many families learn that their '22-karat' gold holds less gold than they paid for. They are upset, but they still own that jewellery and don't know what to do with it.
Your machines have shown many families that their '22-karat' gold holds less gold than they paid for. They are upset, but they still own that jewellery and don't know what to do with it.

d5.question: What do you offer them?
d5.advisor: These families have already lost money on their gold. How much of that loss can we afford to carry?

options.label: Swap their 19 to 22-karat pieces for Tanishq 22-karat, and you pay for the missing gold.

outcome.text: You call it Impure to Pure. Old jewellery that tests between 19 and 22 karat can be swapped for 22-karat Tanishq jewellery, and Tanishq pays for the missing gold. It wins families away from their old jewellers. In 2002–03 sales grow by more than a third, profit is more than four times higher, and you have 60 stores in 47 towns.

Old jewellery that tests between 19 and 22 karat can now be swapped for 22-karat Tanishq jewellery. Families pay only the making charge, and Tanishq pays for the missing gold. It costs you a lot, but families start leaving their old jewellers for you.

options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. Switching jewellers felt risky and would have cost families money. You carried that cost, so leaving the old jeweller became the safe choice.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you paid to solve the customer's problem and earned their trust.

options.label: Give every family that tests its gold a ₹500 coupon. It's simple, though you pay even if they never buy.
options.outcome: Some families use the coupon on a small piece. But their old jewellery still holds less gold than they paid for, and most of them take it back to the jeweller they know.
options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. A coupon is a small gift, but the big loss stayed with the family: the gold they had already lost. Few people switch while they still carry that loss.
options.better: Swap their old pieces for your 22-karat gold, and pay for the missing gold yourself.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you gave a small gift, but left buyers carrying the big loss.

options.label: Buy their old gold at its tested value. It's fair and costs you nothing, but families get less back.
options.outcome: The offer is fair, but buyers lose money on the deal. Many leave angry with their old jeweller, but they don't come to you either.
options.why: Remember: take the risk off the buyer. The price was fair, but the buyer still carried the whole loss from someone else's cheating. Few people switch when switching itself costs them money.
options.better: Swap their old pieces for your 22-karat gold, and pay for the missing gold yourself.
options.takeaway: In 2002 you offered a fair price but did not make switching easy.

legend.title: The name India trusts with its gold

text.text: By 2003 Tanishq is one of India's top five retailers, and it goes on to become India's biggest jewellery brand. A plant built for Europe found its buyers in India by proving that its gold was pure.
You learned early what Indian families wanted, and then gave them proof they could see for themselves. Tanishq becomes the name millions of families trust with their gold.
You gave Indian families the gold they wanted and the proof they needed. Tanishq becomes the name millions of families trust with their gold.

survivor.title: A trusted jeweller, but not the biggest

text.text: Tanishq stops losing money and keeps its stores busy in the big cities. But families in smaller towns never get to know it, so they stay with their old jewellers.
Tanishq stops losing money and becomes a respected jeweller. But it never quite wins over the families who stay loyal to their old jeweller, so it remains one good name among many.

collapse.title: The jewellery business is sold
collapse.text: After years of losses, the board no longer wants to keep the jewellery business. Titan sells it and goes back to making watches.

fired.title: The board replaces you
fired.text: After three costly decisions and years of losses, the board puts someone else in charge of the jewellery business.

realHistory: Titan built a jewellery plant to sell to Europe, but the export plan failed. Tanishq opened its first store in 1996 with Western 18-karat diamond jewellery and lost money every year. It moved toward 22-karat gold, and from 1997 its Karatmeter let anyone test their gold free in the store, showing that much '22-karat' jewellery held less gold. After a crisis in 2000, a new team brought buyers in and made the first profit. The Impure to Pure exchange won families from their old jewellers, and Tanishq became India's biggest jewellery brand.
